blogs.title: When Is Terror Not “Persecution”? Jimenez v. Bondi and the Tenth Circuit’s High Bar for Threat-Based Asylum Claims
blogs.description: This post would examine the panel’s conclusion that repeated death threats, armed confrontations at the family business, an assault on an employee, and an apparent attempt to seize the petitioners’ child still did not compel a finding of past persecution. It would explore the tension between the cumulative-harm principle and the court’s continued insistence that threats, psychological trauma, and fear—without clearer physical injury—usually remain insufficient.

blogs.title: Politics or Retaliation? Mixed Motives, Criminal Enterprise, and the Nexus Problem in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: This post would analyze why the court treated the petitioners’ Liberal Party work as merely tangential to the harm they suffered, concluding that Don Rafa’s central motive was to protect his property, revenue, and security from a perceived “snitch.” It would situate the decision within the INA’s “one central reason” framework and ask what it means for asylum claims arising at the intersection of political activism, anti-corruption work, and politically connected organized crime.

blogs.title: Report It or Lose It? Jimenez v. Bondi and the Tenth Circuit’s Demanding View of Government ‘Unable or Unwilling’ Protection
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s heavy emphasis on notice to the state: because the petitioners made only limited, informal reports to individual officers, the panel held the record did not show Colombia was unable or unwilling to protect them. It would discuss the practical and doctrinal stakes of requiring more formal reporting even where applicants credibly fear police corruption or complicity, and why the court treated prior searches of the relevant property as evidence of state willingness.

blogs.title: Safe Somewhere in Colombia? Internal Relocation After Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: This post would explore the panel’s alternative holding that the family could reasonably relocate within Colombia, relying on their three-week stay in the Bogotá countryside, the continued safety of relatives, and the fact that the threats told them to leave the neighborhood rather than the country. It would consider how internal-relocation doctrine can narrow protection in cases involving localized but serious private-actor threats tied to criminal and political networks.
